records.place: Manutuke, by the Te Arai River, Gisborne

wine.name: Millton Te Arai Vineyard Chenin Blanc
wine.sites: The Te Arai Vineyard, the home block on the banks of the Te Arai River near Manutuke, where the house was founded in 1984; autumn mists off the river can bring botrytis in some years.
wine.making: Organically and biodynamically grown fruit is picked by hand in up to four passes through the vineyard, some years ending with a pass for grapes touched by botrytis. The wine is fermented and raised partly in stainless steel tanks and partly in demi-muids, large French oak casks of 600 litres, chosen so that the wood gives texture rather than the taste of oak.
wine.glass: Lime, green apple and quince, with mango in warm years and honey where botrytis has come in; a waxy, textured palate, mouth watering acidity and a softening edge of sweetness on the finish.
wine.ageing: Open and fruity on release; like Chenin Blanc of its weight elsewhere, it can gain honeyed depth over several years in bottle.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a little air helps a young bottle; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: The home block beside the Te Arai River at Manutuke, the wine's single source.
The Geographical Indication of the Poverty Bay region on the North Island's east coast.

records.table: Millton Vineyards and Winery was founded at Manutuke in 1984 and certified organic in 1989, and its Te Arai Vineyard Chenin Blanc comes from the home block by the river: lime, green apple and honey, a waxy texture and bright acidity. Pour it with fish.
records.story: The family's roots in Gisborne wine go back to 1969, when the father of one of the founders planted the Opou Vineyard near Manutuke. In 1984 the young couple founded their own winery on the banks of the Te Arai River near Manutuke, on land where, by the house's account, settlers had first planted vines in 1871. They farmed without synthetic sprays from the start, and in 1989 the estate gained organic certification from BioGro, by the accounts of New Zealand Winegrowers and the local press the first wine producer in the country to do so. Biodynamic farming followed, later certified by Demeter, and the house came to be known abroad as a pioneer of both. Chenin Blanc, rare in New Zealand, became its signature: grown on the riverside home block, where autumn mists off the water can bring botrytis, and raised in large casks of the Loire kind. In 2025, after more than forty vintages, the family announced that the harvest of that year would be its last and that it would retire the vineyard and itself rather than sell, so the Te Arai Chenin Blanc stands as the record of one family's work. For a sommelier it is the Chenin that tells Gisborne's story.

records.place: Matawhero, on the Poverty Bay flats, Gisborne

wine.name: Matawhero Gewürztraminer
wine.sites: The home vineyard at Riverpoint on the Poverty Bay flats, planted in the 1960s, on silt loam over clay that gives the grape its rich, dense fruit.
wine.making: Picked while the fruit is cool, often by machine in the early morning, then carried quickly to the winery and pressed, as the house's vintage notes describe. It is made as a fresh, fruit led white in a dry or nearly dry style.
wine.glass: Lychee, nashi pear and Turkish delight with a touch of ginger; a nearly dry palate, rounded in texture and held by a steely line of acidity, with a long, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Made for drinking young, in the first few years after the vintage, while its perfume is at its height.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with room for the perfume.

records.table: Matawhero, on the Poverty Bay flats, made its name in the 1970s with Gewürztraminer, and its Single Vineyard Gewürztraminer carries that on: lychee, nashi pear and Turkish delight, dry and rounded with a steely line. Pour it with gently spiced dishes.
records.story: In the 1960s a grower planted a vineyard at Matawhero, on the flats outside Gisborne, importing his own vines, among them Gewürztraminer, a grape then almost unknown in the country. His son brought the family's own label to life in 1975, when the first wines appeared under the Matawhero name, and within a few years his Gewürztraminer was winning notice at home and abroad, so that the house became known for wine of its own rather than for grapes sold on. Through the 1970s and 1980s the name Matawhero and the grape Gewürztraminer went together in the minds of the country's wine drinkers, and Gisborne, long the engine of bulk white wine, had a fine aromatic white to show. In 2008 the son sold the winery and vineyard to a local family, who revitalised and replanted the estate and relaunched the label. They later released the Irwin Chardonnay, of the Mendoza clone the father had brought into the country, named in tribute to the father and son who had founded the house. In 2025 Matawhero marked fifty years since its first wines. For a sommelier its Gewürztraminer is the link between Gisborne's pioneering years and its later wines.

wine.name: Vinoptima Ormond Reserve Gewürztraminer
wine.sites: The estate's own vineyard on Ngakoroa Road at Ormond, inland from Gisborne, planted to Gewürztraminer alone: a first block in 2000 and a second in 2007.
wine.making: The estate made Gewürztraminer and nothing else. The Reserve was an off dry wine of full weight, its fruit and perfume intense enough to make it seem sweeter than it was, and a late harvest wine was made beside it from the same vineyard.
wine.glass: Rose and Turkish delight over honey and ripe pear; full bodied and off dry, its fruit and flowers so intense that it seems sweeter than it is, with a long and heavily perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Built to last longer than most Gewürztraminer; the bottles that remain are older vintages, so taste one before pouring it for a guest.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with room for the perfume.

records.table: Vinoptima Estate was founded at Ormond in 2000 to make Gewürztraminer alone, and the Ormond Reserve Gewürztraminer was its principal wine: off dry, rich and perfumed with rose and Turkish delight. The estate went into receivership in 2018, so older bottles are all that remain.
records.story: The founder came from the family behind the Nobilo winery at Huapai, north west of Auckland. In 2000 he founded Vinoptima Estate at Ormond, inland from Gisborne, to make Gewürztraminer and nothing else. The first wines followed a few years after the planting, and the Ormond Reserve, with a late harvest wine beside it, became the estate's calling card: rich, off dry and made to age. A second block was planted in 2007. But the wine sold more slowly than it was made, and a stock of about a hundred thousand litres of Gewürztraminer built up in the cellar. In 2018 a secured creditor called in the receivers, the stock was offered for sale by tender, and the vineyard and winery were later sold. Vinoptima no longer makes wine. For a sommelier the Ormond Reserve is a lesson in two things at once: what Gisborne's warm, fertile flats can give Gewürztraminer, and how hard it is to build a house on one grape alone.

wine.name: TW Chardonnay
wine.sites: The two founding growers' neighbouring vineyards on Back Ormond Road, in the foothills from Ormond to Hexton north of Gisborne, a strip the locals call the Golden Slope after the Côte d'Or.
wine.making: Fermented in barriques of French and American oak, with Hungarian oak in some years, partly with indigenous yeast. The wine then goes through full malolactic fermentation, which gives it its creamy texture, and is fined, stabilised, filtered and bottled, as the house's technical notes describe.
wine.glass: Ripe peach and nectarine with grapefruit, over butterscotch, toasted nuts and vanilla from the barrels; full and creamy, with soft acidity and a long, rounded finish.
wine.ageing: Rich and ready on release; it holds for a few years as the fruit turns nutty, but it is made to be drunk rather than laid down.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a wide white wine glass.

records.table: TW Wines began in 1998, when two Gisborne growers set out to bottle fruit from their own vineyards, and its Reserve Gisborne Chardonnay is the barrel fermented one: ripe peach, butterscotch and toasted nuts, made creamy by malolactic. Pour it with roast chicken or crayfish.
records.story: Gisborne grew Chardonnay for decades before most of its growers made wine of their own, and much of its fruit went to the large wineries. Two growers whose neighbouring vineyards lay on Back Ormond Road, on the foothills the locals call the Golden Slope, wanted a label of their own. In 1997, on a fishing trip to Lake Waikaremoana, they hatched the idea, and they named it simply with the initials of their two families. Advised by local winemakers, they aimed at the next vintage, formed a company, found space in a winery and made their first wines in 1998. The range grew from there: an unoaked Estate Chardonnay, the barrel fermented Reserve, a Chardonnay and Viognier blend, and red wines of Malbec and Merlot. It was built as a small grower's label, a fair picture of a region where the vineyard comes first. For a sommelier the TW Reserve Chardonnay shows the warm, generous Gisborne style that gave the region its name for Chardonnay.

wine.sites: Bought in fruit blended for the house style, never one vineyard: New Zealand listings give Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, while the brand's own Classic Brut page gives South Australia, so read the back label.

The sources read do not settle the method of the Classic: the brand describes its Special Reserve as bottle fermented with two years on its lees, and a New Zealand guide notes that many Lindauer wines are made in tank.
wine.glass: Lemon, green apple and white peach with a light bready note; a lively mousse, crisp acidity and a clean, dry, simple finish.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, within a year or two, while the fruit is fresh; it gains nothing from keeping.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a tulip shaped glass or a flute.

records.table: Lindauer is the sparkling brand Montana launched for Christmas 1981, named after the painter Gottfried Lindauer, and Classic Brut Cuvée is its core wine: a dry, non vintage blend of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, crisp and lemony. Pour it well chilled.
records.story: The name is a painter's. Gottfried Lindauer (1839 to 1926) was born at Pilsen in Bohemia, sailed for New Zealand in 1874 and settled at Woodville, where he painted the portraits of Māori for which he is known; he died there in 1926. In 1981 Montana Wines launched a sparkling wine under his name for Christmas, and the brand grew into a familiar bottle at home and abroad. Montana's own fortunes ran through the sales of the wine trade: it passed to Allied Domecq in 2001 and, with Allied, to Pernod Ricard in 2005. In 2010 Pernod Ricard sold Lindauer, with several other New Zealand brands, to a consortium of Lion Nathan and Indevin; Indevin took the Lindauer winery in Gisborne and the vineyards, and came to make the wine under contract. Montana itself later took the name Brancott Estate, so the two stories part there. The brand's own pages give Gisborne and Hawke's Bay for its Special Reserve and South Australia for the Classic Brut Cuvée. For a sommelier it is a lesson to read the back label: a name born in Gisborne need not mean Gisborne fruit.

others.note: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from Gisborne and Hawke's Bay, bottle fermented and aged on its lees for two years, by the brand's account.

others.name: Lindauer Free Brut
others.note: An alcohol free wine of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from the same two regions.

traps: Lindauer is a brand, not an estate: it has no single vineyard, and its name is a painter's, not a place.
Lindauer began as Montana's brand but left Pernod Ricard in 2010; Brancott Estate, Montana's later name, is a separate house.
The Special Reserve, not the Classic, is the Lindauer the brand describes as bottle fermented with two years on its lees.

cards.front: Lindauer: after whom is the brand named?
cards.back: Gottfried Lindauer, the Bohemian born painter of Māori portraits who settled at Woodville.

cards.front: Which wine company launched Lindauer in 1981?
cards.back: Montana Wines, the company that later took the name Brancott Estate.

questions.q: A guest asks which grapes go into Lindauer Classic Brut Cuvée. What do you say?

questions.exp: The brand gives Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, the grapes of Champagne; Sauvignon Blanc is the grape New Zealand plants most, but it plays no part in this blend.

questions.q: In 2010 Pernod Ricard sold the Lindauer brand. Who bought it?
opts: A consortium of Lion Nathan and Indevin
The Champagne house of Deutz
The Allied Domecq group of Britain
A co-operative of Gisborne growers
questions.exp: Pernod Ricard sold Lindauer to Lion Nathan and Indevin in 2010; Allied Domecq had owned Montana from 2001 until Pernod Ricard took it over in 2005.

report: Pick in doubt, kept: the brand's own Classic Brut page describes a blend of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from South Australia, while its Brut Cuvée page and a Falstaff listing (Lindauer Classic Gisborne Hawkes Bay Brut Cuvée) give Gisborne and Hawke's Bay. The record follows the latter two; the integrator should confirm which bottle the label means, and a swap to a Gisborne estate (Bushmere Estate or Kirkpatrick Estate) is offered if the Gisborne link is only history.

The method is in conflict: one search summary of the brand's site says many Lindauer wines are made in tank and the vintage wine is the traditional method exception, while an importer and a New Zealand merchant describe the Brut as bottle fermented with twelve to eighteen months on lees. The record says traditional method by those accounts; the checker should settle it.

The launch of 1981 rests on the brand's own Since 1981 and on Tastingbook; the claim that it was the first commercial traditional method wine of the country and the 1980 harvest of Gisborne and Hawke's Bay base wine rest on Tastingbook alone and are left out.
The sale price of 2010 differs by source and is not given; the brand's owners after 2010 are not followed.
Gottfried Lindauer's dates, Pilsen, 1874 and Woodville rest on Te Ara and Wikipedia.
The closing line on Gisborne's role as the source of sparkling base wine draws on the region record and the brand's current Gisborne and Hawke's Bay sourcing; the checker may soften it.
The winemaker named on the brand's site is living and never named.

changed: wine.sites and appellation: Gisborne and Hawke's Bay alone; now both accounts, the brand's own Classic Brut page giving South Australia (lindauer.co.nz, two searches) against Falstaff and Cuisine's listings. The author's primary source, the Brut Cuvée page, is the Special Reserve's.

wine.making: the traditional method with a year or more on lees; now the method unsettled: the brand gives bottle fermentation and two years on lees for the Special Reserve only, and Cuisine says many Lindauer wines are made in tank.

table and story: bottle fermented and from Gisborne and Hawke's Bay cut; the launch now for Christmas 1981 (Drinks International, Wine Searcher's brand page); the buyers of 2010 now a consortium of Lion Nathan and Indevin, Indevin taking the Gisborne winery and vineyards and making the wine under contract (Drinks International, Harpers).

story: the rename to Brancott Estate in the same year told without a year here (wave one's Marlborough record gives from 2010); the closing on Gisborne's role as the source of sparkling base wine cut, in no source read, for the lesson of the back label.
questions: the wine question on the bottle's second fermentation replaced by the grapes, the method being unsettled; a trap added on the Special Reserve.
wine.glass: toast and vanilla cut, in no source read for the Classic.
sources: Tastingbook and Wikipedia cut; the brand's Classic Brut page, Drinks International and Cuisine added.
open: Swap accepted (see the review file): the flagship's Gisborne link is history and its fruit by the brand's own page is South Australian, so this record stands only until the read together agent applies the swap.
Which bottling the New Zealand market's Classic Brut Cuvée is, and its method, could not be settled.
